newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -GEAR UP FOR GILT GAINS AT LONG END.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -GEAR UP FOR GILT GAINS AT LONG END.

text.p: British gilts have scope to outperform German debt over the medium term though a mixed Bank of England inflation report will do little to speed up that process, economists said on Wednesday.

With lingering uncertainty over the degree of rate tightening needed to slow the economy, analysts suggested investors plump for the long end of the curve, particularly as real yields are relatively attractive.

"I still think gilts have the scope to outperform further from current levels versus Germany, but I don't think this report is a reason to rush out and buy them," said Joanne Collins, senior market strategist at Nomura International in London.
The Bank of England said in its quarterly inflation report on Wednesday that a pause in UK monetary policy should be possible as it assesses the inflation outlook.
But how long will that pause be, and will it merely be the prelude to another rate rise? Analysts were unsure and divided over the amount of value left in the gilt yield curve.
Steve Scott, gilts analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson, said he would be reluctant to get into the short end of the curve.

"The Bank is probably hoping this pause will be for four to six months -- but we might get to October...and find inflation pressures are stronger than expected so rates will have to go to 7.25 percent," he said.
"So I'd be a bit negative on the shorter end of the gilt curve, which suggests the yield curve will flatten up again." Scott suggested investors put on lengthening trades in that environment.

The Bank raised official interest rates last week, for the fourth time since May, by 25 basis points to 7.0 percent. It said at the time there was a "perception interest rates have reached a level consistent with the inflation target".
Scott expected the gilt/Bund spread to narrow over the medium term, although he added the impetus was more likely to come from Bund weakness than gilt strength.
He saw the gilt/Bund gap narrowing from its present 150 basis points to 120 by the end of the year.
Jan Loeys, global fixed income strategist at J.P. Morgan in London, also favoured the long end of the gilt curve, predicting further inversion in future.
He said interest rates may need to rise as much as another 100 basis points, and the short end would need to adjust.
"The long end won't get hurt as much because the Bank of England has acquired some credibility -- people are more confident any inflation pressures will be contained," he said.
Loeys said investors were attracted to the longer end because of decent nominal and real yields, and because of concern over frothiness in equity markets.
Collins was more benign over the interest rate outlook and suggested the five year sector of the curve was the best place to be.
"There's probably scope to steepen from the short end because that's still probably pricing in too much interest rate tightening," she said.
"So I'd still be in five year. That part of the curve has been cheap, it's still cheap, and it has the potential to benefit from further reassesment of the interest rate outlook."
